question.stem: A tram stores energy in a flywheel, a uniform disc of mass 300 kg and radius 0.40 m that spins about its central axis. The moment of inertia of a uniform disc is $I = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$. At full speed the flywheel rotates at 3000 $\text{rev min}^{-1}$.
question.diagramAlt: A uniform disc of mass M seen face on, with its radius R drawn from the centre to the edge and a curved arrow showing it spinning with angular speed omega about its centre.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.question: Show that the moment of inertia of the flywheel is about 24 $\text{kg m}^{2}$.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.question: Calculate the rotational kinetic energy of the flywheel at full speed.
markscheme: $\omega = \dfrac{3000 \times 2\pi}{60} = 314\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$ ✓
$E_{\text{k}} = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = 1.18 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}$; allow ECF from (a)(i) ✓

mistakes.feedback: Convert the rotation rate to an angular speed in rad s⁻¹: multiply revolutions per second by 2π.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.question: The tram is parked and the flywheel is left spinning freely from full speed. The only torque on it is a constant frictional torque of 0.80 $\text{N m}$ in the bearings. Determine the time taken for the flywheel to stop.
markscheme: $\alpha = \dfrac{\tau}{I} = 0.0333\ \text{rad s}^{-2}$ ✓
$t = \dfrac{\omega}{\alpha} = 9420\ \text{s}$; allow ECF from (a)(i) and (a)(ii) ✓

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.question: Calculate the number of revolutions the flywheel makes while it slows down to rest.
markscheme: $\Delta\theta = \dfrac{\omega_{\text{i}} + \omega_{\text{f}}}{2}t$ (OR $\omega_{\text{i}}^2 = 2\alpha\Delta\theta$) ✓
number of revolutions $= \dfrac{\Delta\theta}{2\pi} = 2.36 \times 10^{5}$; allow ECF from (a)(iii) ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: The flywheel is used to accelerate the tram, of mass $1.8 \times 10^{4}$ kg, from rest to 6.0 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ on level track. During this time the flywheel slows from 3000 $\text{rev min}^{-1}$ to 2400 $\text{rev min}^{-1}$. Determine the efficiency of this energy transfer.
markscheme: energy given up by the flywheel $= \tfrac{1}{2}I(\omega_1^2 - \omega_2^2) = 4.26 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}$ ✓
kinetic energy gained by the tram $= \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = 3.24 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}$ ✓
$\eta = \dfrac{3.24 \times 10^{5}}{4.26 \times 10^{5}} = 0.76$; allow ECF from (a)(i) ✓

mistakes.feedback: Use the energy the flywheel actually gave up (from the change in its rotation rate), not all the energy it stored.

parts.label: c(i)
parts.question: The flywheel turns a rectangular generator coil of 200 turns and area 0.020 $\text{m}^{2}$ in a uniform magnetic field of strength 0.35 T. The coil turns at the same rate as the flywheel at full speed. Determine the average emf induced while the coil turns through a quarter of a revolution, starting from the position where the flux linkage is greatest.
markscheme: change in flux linkage $= NBA$, in a time of a quarter of a period, $\dfrac{1}{4f}$ with $f = 50\ \text{Hz}$ ✓
$\varepsilon = \dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = 4NBAf = 280\ \text{V}$ ✓

parts.label: c(ii)
parts.question: Explain how the emf from the generator changes as the flywheel slows down.
markscheme: the flux linkage changes more slowly, so the peak (maximum) emf decreases ✓
and its frequency decreases: each cycle of the emf takes longer ✓

parts.label: c(iii)
parts.question: Explain, with reference to Lenz's law, why the flywheel slows down more quickly when the generator supplies a current.
markscheme: the induced current opposes the change that produces it, so the forces on the coil produce a torque opposing the rotation ✓
the electrical energy supplied comes from the kinetic energy of the flywheel (energy is conserved), so it loses energy faster ✓

parts.label: d(i)
parts.question: Explain, in terms of the particles of the steel, why the bearings warm up as the flywheel slows down.
markscheme: work done against friction transfers energy to the bearings ✓
increasing the random kinetic energy of the particles of the steel, so the internal energy and temperature increase ✓

parts.label: d(ii)
parts.question: The bearings and their steel housing have a total mass of 45 kg. Steel has a specific heat capacity of 450 $\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$. Calculate the rise in temperature of the bearings and housing when the flywheel runs down from full speed to rest, assuming no energy leaves them.
markscheme: $Q = mc\Delta T$ with $Q$ = the energy stored at full speed ✓
$\Delta T = 58.5\ \text{K}$; allow ECF from (a)(ii) ✓

M.what: mass of the flywheel (a uniform disc)

w1.what: full rotation rate of the flywheel

w2.what: rotation rate of the flywheel after accelerating the tram

N.what: number of turns on the generator coil

B.what: magnetic field strength in the generator

mb.what: mass of the bearings and their steel housing

parts.label: a(i)
parts.examinerNote: The equation is given, as the guide requires for a particular shape.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.examinerNote: The angular speed must be in rad s⁻¹.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.examinerNote: Newton's second law for rotation, then uniform angular deceleration (or angular impulse τt = Iω).

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.examinerNote: Angular displacement in radians, divided by 2π.

parts.label: b
parts.examinerNote: Efficiency = useful energy out / energy in. The flywheel does not stop, so only the change in its energy counts.

parts.label: c(i)
parts.examinerNote: Faraday's law for an average emf: the flux linkage falls from NBA to zero in a quarter turn. Sign ignored (magnitude).

parts.label: c(ii)
parts.examinerNote: Both the amplitude and the frequency of the sinusoidal emf fall with the rotation rate.

parts.label: c(iii)
parts.examinerNote: Lenz's law as a consequence of energy conservation; with no current there is no opposing magnetic torque.

parts.label: d(i)
parts.examinerNote: Temperature is a measure of the average random kinetic energy of the particles.

parts.label: d(ii)
parts.examinerNote: All the rotational kinetic energy is dissipated in the bearings. In practice energy leaves by conduction and radiation, so the real rise is smaller.
